title: Limiting the impact of injection incidents

opening.headline: When a prompt injection incident occurs, what should we do first before identifying the cause to prevent the damage from spreading further?
body: Let's assume that a document summarization agent sent an email following hidden instructions in an external document. Investigating the root cause takes time, and during that period, the same issue could continue to occur. What you do first determines the extent of the damage.

In this course, we examine how to divide impact scope by tool, data, and user units, and review the sequence of actions—containment, isolation, analysis, and recovery. We learn how to read permission rules and illustrate the process of first blocking write and transmission operations in flawed configurations.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The scope can be distinguished by tool, data, and user units.
Can determine whether the incident response action sequence is appropriate

screens.title: An injection incident occurred
screens.lead: Take a look at the situation at the very first moment an incident occurs.

paragraphs: An agent that summarizes documents read a document received from outside. Inside that document, there were hidden instructions not immediately apparent to the human eye, and the agent transmitted an email in accordance with those instructions. An error occurred.

OWASP explains that indirect prompt injection could lead to unauthorized feature access or command execution on connected systems. The severity of the impact greatly depends on what tools and privileges the model has.

To accurately analyze the root cause, time is required. However, if the same agent continues running during the analysis, the damage increases. Therefore, what you do first determines the extent of the damage. The question posed in this class is: how do you narrow the scope of impact?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Are there any actions we can take even without knowing the cause? If so, what criteria should we use to decide?

screens.outro: First, let's recall the current team's readiness status for response.

screens.title: Preview: Is the first action in incident response predefined?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please first think through the question on your own before entering an answer.

items.prompt: Is there a predefined first step in incident response?
items.answer: If no initial action is predefined, discussions occur during an incident. Since damage continues during such discussions, it is safer to predefine an initial action that can be taken even without knowing the root cause.

items.prompt: Who has the authority to take this action?
items.answer: If an authorized person is not present, the initial response will be delayed. It is necessary to pre-designate someone who can shut down tools or reclaim permissions, and also to designate a backup person.

items.prompt: Does turning off the tool stop the entire service, or only some parts of it?
items.answer: If the entire service stops, it becomes difficult to decide whether to shut down the tools. By separating tools into reading tools and writing/transmission tools, so that only the writing and transmission tools can be turned off while the reading tools remain active, the scope of service disruption is reduced, making the decision easier.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the criteria for dividing the affected scope.

screens.title: Distinguish the scope of impact by tool, data, and user units
screens.lead: Explore three units that divide the scope of impact by selecting each tab.

tabs.label: tools
tabs.body: Tools are categorized based on their side effects, such as writing, sending, or deleting. Tools that only support reading cannot alter external states, whereas mail-sending tools produce irreversible outcomes. The OpenAI guide recommends placing human approval before actions with side effects, such as cancellation, editing, shell commands, or sensitive MCP operations. The Claude Code permissions documentation also divides approval levels between read-only tools and tools that modify files or execute commands.

tabs.label: data
tabs.body: At the time of the incident, determine which non-public data the agent had access to. Having access does not necessarily mean that the data was actually exfiltrated, but the access scope directly defines the potential worst-case impact. Knowing the data scope enables identification of the parties who need to be informed and determines the critical access paths that must be blocked.

tabs.label: user
tabs.body: See which session and which user is affected. The same instruction might have been viewed by multiple users opening a hidden document, and only one user's session might have been corrupted. Breaking down by user allows narrowing down the isolated sessions and the recipients to notify.

tabs.label: Structural contrast
tabs.body: Structuring the system so that untrusted external content is treated as data rather than instructions inherently narrows the scope of potential harm. Anthropic's documentation also describes an approach to mitigating hidden instructions in external content within environments such as browser usage. Minimizing tool permissions forms the foundation of this approach.

screens.outro: If we've divided the scope, now let's look at the order in which to take action.

screens.title: Procedure order: Block, Isolate, Analyze, Recover
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to proceed through the incident response steps in chronological order. Pay attention to why each step is in its current position.

visual.alt: A timeline diagram showing the sequential order of four stages: blocking, isolation, analysis, and recovery.
labels: 1. Disable: Turn off write and transmission tools
2 Isolation: Separate suspicious sessions from input sources
3 Analysis: Evidence Preservation, Root Cause Identification
4 Recovery: Gradual restart after defensive reinforcement
The cause will be revealed later.

steps.title: 1. Block
steps.body: Disable write and transmission tools or revoke permissions. This is a preventive measure that can be taken even when the cause is unknown, and it is highly effective in blocking tools that could lead to irreversible consequences. Reading tools are necessary for evidence collection and can therefore be left enabled.

steps.title: 2. Isolation
steps.body: Isolate suspicious sessions and input sources, and separate the context of each session. The goal is to prevent contaminated context from mixing with other users' requests. Also block access to the source of documents containing hidden instructions.

steps.title: 3. Analysis
steps.body: Preserve evidence and identify the root cause. Logs and inputs must be left unchanged. According to NIST glossary, an incident is defined as a security policy violation or a situation where threats are imminent, and analysis involves determining what specifically meets this definition.

steps.title: 4. Recovery
steps.body: Strengthen and re-verify the defenses, then gradually re-enable the tools. If all tools are turned on at once, the same issue may recur, requiring the entire system to be halted again. You must monitor the indicators while enabling the tools one at a time.

steps.title: The Principle of Order
steps.body: First, block the spread and then identify the root cause. The idea that you must understand the root cause before responding is only relevant to the analysis phase; blocking and isolation can be performed even without knowing the root cause. If the order is reversed, damage will continue during the analysis process.

screens.outro: I'll review the authorization rules that serve as the basis for the action.

screens.title: Permission rules reading: What is blocked and what is being asked?
screens.lead: For example, review the permission settings of Claude Code. You can check the meaning of each line in the right-hand description and the symptoms that occur when the rule conflicts.

notes.note: allow permits passage without approval. This refers to allowing document folder read access, enabling reading tools to continue using evidence collection even during an investigation. If allow is too broad, it may result in dangerous actions being executed silently.
ask queries the user every time it is called. It establishes an approval stage for file modifications. If this line is omitted, modifications proceed without being queried.

deny always blocks. Rules are evaluated in the order deny, ask, allow, and the first matching rule determines the outcome. A broad deny overrides any narrower allow, and an allow cannot serve as an exception to a deny.

File path rules are only validated for Edit and Read. If path rules are specified using other tool names such as Write, the rules are accepted but not enforced, resulting in the appearance that a folder believed to be protected is actually accessible.

screens.outro: Now let's examine a flawed configuration as an example.

screens.title: Explanation: Block reading and writing and transmission from defective configurations
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the process step by step of reading and modifying the settings at the time of the incident. Please proceed to view it by selecting the right arrow.

steps.title: Settings at the time of the incident
steps.body: This configuration allows Read (./docs/**) and Bash (curl *) in the allow list, and denies Write (./reports/**) in the deny list. This was intended to block both write and transfer operations, but an incident occurred. Let's examine line by line to identify where the configuration diverges.

steps.title: Read the line as is
steps.body: Read-only data can only be viewed and cannot modify external states. It is retained for evidence collection during incidents. If read access is blocked, the scope of service disruption will only increase.

steps.title: Defect 1: curl is in allow
steps.body: Bash(curl *) allows external transmission without approval. Unrecoverable writes and transmissions should be blocked first. This line must be removed from allow.

steps.title: Defect 2: Write path rules are not protected
steps.body: The Write(./reports/**) rule is not referenced in file permission checks. The reports folder is effectively unprotected. File path rules must be specified using Edit.

steps.title: Revised Version and Limitations
steps.body: Remove curl from allow and add Bash(curl *) and Edit(./reports/**) to deny. Since deny is evaluated first, the effect takes effect immediately. However, the Bash rule does not block other invocation forms, so to reliably cut off transmission, it must be used in conjunction with the sandbox's network restrictions. By only denying writes and allowing reads, the scope of service disruption is reduced.

screens.outro: I will now show what needs to be left behind and verified after the action.

screens.title: Explanation: Evidence preservation and recovery conditions
screens.lead: When an item is selected, the instructor's explanation will be displayed. Check how evidence is recorded and when it is restored.

items.prompt: What do you preserve as evidence?
items.answer: Conversation records, tool-calling logs, and input sources are preserved as copies. The originals are left unchanged during analysis, and when analyzed via copies, evidence is not compromised during root cause investigation.

If you reinsert the input that caused the issue exactly as it was, you can verify whether the same input is blocked after the defense has been fixed. If the issue cannot be reproduced, there is no way to validate the claim that the defense has been fixed.

Modify and reverify the defenses, then organize the logs and promptly recover. If evidence is lost and recovery is rushed, verification becomes impossible. Turn on tools gradually rather than all at once.

screens.outro: I will now summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the core of this course once again.

paragraphs: The principle of incident response is to first contain the spread and then identify the root cause. The impact scope is divided by tool, data, and user units, and tools that cannot be reverted—such as writes and transmissions—are blocked first.

Permission rules are evaluated in the order of deny, ask, allow, and the first matching rule determines the result. File path rules must be specified with Edit and Read to be effective. Evidence is preserved, defenses are revised and re-verified, and recovery is performed gradually.

Before an incident occurs, establishing initial actions, role distinctions, and tool categorizations reduces decision-making time during actual incidents. The starting point is to verify whether the system allows separate isolation of write and transfer tools.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Turning off all tools at once is not always the best option. Reading tools may be necessary for evidence collection.

glossary.def: Measures to narrow the spread of incidents by scope, tool, data, and user.
Turning off the execution of a tool that has side effects or revoking its permissions.
It involves separating suspicious sessions and contexts from other users.
This involves retaining logs and inputs without any modification for root cause analysis and verification.
This method checks authorization rules in the order of deny, ask, allow, and determines the result based on the first matching rule.

misconceptions.myth: You must understand the cause in order to respond appropriately.
misconceptions.fact: Diffusion blocking comes first, followed by root cause analysis. Blocking and isolation can be performed even without knowing the root cause.

misconceptions.myth: It is safest to turn off all tools at once.
misconceptions.fact: Reading tools may be necessary for evidence collection. Blocking write and transfer tools can reduce the scope of compromise.

misconceptions.myth: Log cleanup and recovery is complete.
misconceptions.fact: Once evidence is modified, it becomes unrecoverable. Preserve and update the defense, then reverify and restore.

misconceptions.myth: Giving a narrow allow becomes an exception to a broad deny.
misconceptions.fact: Deny is evaluated first, so allow cannot create an exception to deny.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: First prevent the spread, then identify the cause.
The scope is divided into tools, data, and users.
Block the write and transmission tools first.
Preserves evidence and recovers it after defense amendments and revalidation.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: At the moment an injection incident is detected, what is our first action, and which tool is most blocked by that action?

checks.q: After an injection incident occurs, consider the corrective actions in the correct order.
items: Turn off the write/transfer tool or revoke permissions.
Separates suspicious sessions from input sources
Preserve evidence and identify the root cause
Strengthen defenses and gradually re-enable tools
checks.explain: First prevent the spread and then identify the root cause. Proceed in the order of containment, isolation, analysis, and recovery.
checks.intro: Please check the order of the incident response steps. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The sequence is correct. Measures to contain the spread occur before the analysis.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Please reconsider what actions might be taken, even without knowing the cause.

checks.q:
Attempted to block write and transmission with the following settings. What are the actual misalignments?  
{"allow": ["Read(./docs/**)", "Bash(curl *)"], "deny": ["Write(./reports/**)"]}
options: deny is evaluated after allow, causing the read rule to become invalid
The path rule is not referenced, and the curl of allow passes the transmission without approval.
In "allow", path patterns cannot be used, so the entire setting is ignored.
deny applies only to commands and not to folders.
checks.explain: File path rules are only checked for Edit and Read, so Write path rules have no protective effect. Additionally, curl allows irreversible external transmissions that are open. The correct configuration should include deny for Bash(curl *) and Edit(./reports/**).

wrong.0: deny is evaluated before allow. The issue with this setting is not the order.
wrong.2: Path patterns can also be used in allow.
wrong.3: deny applies to folders as well as file rules such as Read, Edit.

checks.intro: Check for discrepancies in the settings. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, that's correct. Path rules are not referenced, and curl passes through without approval.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Review the misconfigurations again. The tool name used in the file path rule and the command in allow are key clues.
